hypotheses.text: A clinical triad consisting of severe intellectual disability, hyperkinetic movement disorders (such as chorea, dystonia, or complex hyperkinesia), and episodic respiratory dysrhythmia (hyperventilation and/or sleep apnea) provides greater than 80% diagnostic specificity in distinguishing RNU2-2-associated DEE from RNU4-2-associated ReNU syndrome.
hypotheses.rationale: While both RNU2-2 DEE and RNU4-2 ReNU syndrome manifest with severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, and intractable epilepsy, prominent hyperkinetic movement disorders and episodic hyperventilation/sleep apnea are recurrently emphasized in RNU2-2 cohorts (Chiu et al., Krygier et al., Henry et al.) but are absent from the cardinal clinical presentation of RNU4-2, which instead features midline stereotypies, autism spectrum behaviors, and generalized hypotonia.

evidence.text: Patients with RNU2-2 DEE had median seizure onset age of 24 months, focal and generalized seizures, status epilepticus (5/5), severe to profound impairment, hyperventilation (3/5), and obstructive sleep apnea (3/5).

hypotheses.text: Episodic hyperventilation is a selective phenotypic discriminator of dominant de novo RNU2-2 DEE, occurring in >50% of dominant cases but <10% of recessive biallelic RNU2-2 cases and <2% of RNU4-2 cases.
hypotheses.rationale: Chiu et al. and Krygier et al. noted episodic hyperventilation in dominant de novo RNU2-2 cases (preceding movement disorders or seizures in 3/5 cases in Chiu et al.), whereas large-scale cohort studies delineating recessive biallelic RNU2-2 cases (Jackson et al., Leitão et al., Henry et al.) observe generalized cerebral atrophy, refractory seizures, and hyperkinesia/sleep problems without high rates of episodic central hyperventilation.

evidence.text: Biallelic RNU2-2 manifests clinically as a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with intellectual disability, cerebral atrophy, absence/refractory seizures, movement disorders, and self-injurious behaviour.

hypotheses.text: The combination of hippocampal sclerosis on brain MRI and sleep-activated multifocal epileptiform discharges is present in >50% of dominant RNU2-2 DEE individuals, distinguishing them from RNU4-2 ReNU syndrome where structural hippocampal sclerosis is virtually absent.
hypotheses.rationale: Chiu et al. observed hippocampal sclerosis on brain MRI in 3 out of 5 patients and sleep-activated multifocal epileptiform discharges on EEG in 4 out of 5 patients with dominant RNU2-2 variants. This neuroimaging and electrophysiological signature is not part of the described spectrum for RNU4-2 (which typically exhibits generalized cerebral atrophy or delayed myelination without mesial temporal sclerosis) or recessive RNU2-2 (characterized by diffuse cerebral atrophy).

evidence.text: In 5 patients with RNU2-2 DEE, electroencephalography showed sleep-activated multifocal epileptiform discharges in 4 patients and hippocampal sclerosis on magnetic resonance imaging in 3 patients.

new_directions.question_text: What is the systematic prevalence and semiology of movement disorders (e.g. choreoathetosis, dystonia, tremor) across the 35 dominant and 91 recessive RNU2-2 cases reported by Leitão et al. compared directly to RNU4-2 cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: Krygier et al. and Henry et al. point to hyperkinesia as a hallmark, but systematic counts per cohort across the Leitão et al. 141 individuals are required to establish true diagnostic sensitivity and specificity.

new_directions.question_text: Does sleep-activated epileptiform discharge or electrical status epilepticus in sleep (ESES/CSWS) correlate specifically with hippocampal sclerosis and respiratory dysrhythmias in dominant RNU2-2 DEE?
new_directions.rationale: Chiu et al. documented sleep-activated epileptiform discharges in 4/5 and status epilepticus in 5/5, suggesting a distinct sleep-epilepsy-autonomic circuit vulnerability in RNU2-2 not shared with other spliceosomopathies.
